items.definition: A set of interlocking terms accounting standards use to define what 'fair value' means when marking an asset or liability to market.
items.core_idea: Fair value is the cash amount an orderly, willing, knowledgeable counterparty would pay or receive for an asset/liability at the measurement date; several supporting definitions (exit price, market participant, orderly market, active market) pin down exactly what 'orderly' and 'willing' mean.
key_points: Exit price: what would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants, as of the measurement date.
Fair value: the cash amount corresponding to that exit price; for a single asset/liability it's essentially the same as exit price, but for a quantity it's exit price multiplied by quantity.
Market participant: an independent counterparty who knows current prices/market info, is able to transact, and is willing (not compelled) to transact.
Orderly market: one where participants have adequate time to complete a transaction.

Active market: one where transactions occur often enough and in enough volume to give continuous pricing information — a distinct concept from 'orderly', and fair value depends on the market being orderly, not necessarily active.

Orderly/active are properties of the market for a specific asset or liability (e.g., a specific futures contract), not of a trading venue as a whole (e.g., an exchange can have both active and inactive markets within it).
relationships: Because exit price only requires an orderly (not active) market, illiquid assets/liabilities without regular pricing data must still be marked to market — this is the rationale for the fair value hierarchy (level 1-3 inputs).
trading_implications: Marking illiquid positions still requires a fair value estimate even absent frequent trading, so long as a transaction could occur in an orderly manner.
common_misunderstandings: Active and orderly are not the same requirement — a market can be orderly (fair value usable) without being active (frequently traded).

items.topic: Principal market vs. most advantageous market
items.definition: Rules for choosing which market's prices to use for fair value when more than one market for an asset/liability could apply.
items.core_idea: Traders must use the principal market's prices when one exists; only in its absence do they fall back to the most advantageous market (or highest and best use for nonfinancial assets), though in practice the principal market is usually also the most advantageous one.
key_points: Principal market: the market with the greatest volume/activity level for the asset or liability.

Most advantageous market: absent a principal market, the market that maximizes sale proceeds or minimizes liability-transfer cost, net of transaction and transport costs; applies to financial products.

Highest and best use: for nonfinancial assets (e.g., an oil well, pipeline, wind farm), the legally permissible, physically possible, and financially feasible use that maximizes the value of the asset or the group of assets/liabilities it's used within — the nonfinancial-asset analogue of 'most advantageous market', but it does allow consideration of the surrounding business use, unlike most-advantageous-market.
If a principal market exists, its prices govern the mark; if not, the trader must determine highest and best use or the most advantageous market instead.
The primary market is typically (though not always) also the most advantageous market.
relationships: This hierarchy of market selection feeds directly into which price is used as the 'exit price' for fair value.
trading_implications: A trader can't simply pick a favorable price from any market they participate in — they must default to the principal market's price if one exists.
common_misunderstandings: Highest and best use and most advantageous market are similar but not interchangeable — highest and best use applies to nonfinancial assets and factors in the related business, while most advantageous market applies to financial products and does not.

items.definition: Criteria for identifying when a transaction's price should be excluded from fair value determination because the trade itself wasn't orderly.
items.core_idea: Published market prices must generally be used for fair value, but prices from distressed or forced transactions are excluded because those transactions are considered disorderly rather than reflective of a genuine willing-participant price.
key_points: Insufficient marketing time: a trade may be disorderly if it wasn't exposed to the market for the customary period given similar trades under current conditions.

Single buyer: marketing the asset to only one participant can make the trade disorderly, even with a normal marketing period; however, showing the trade to multiple buyers where only one turns out interested is NOT disorderly.
Distressed sale: seller is in or near bankruptcy, facing severe cash shortage, or has assets being repossessed by creditors.

Forced sale: seller must sell to meet legal/regulatory requirements, including under a supervisory agreement with regulators; a firm's own internal risk-limit-driven liquidation policy does NOT count as a forced sale.

Outlier/erroneous price: a transaction price that is an obvious anomaly versus other recent comparable trades (e.g., a misplaced decimal); an unusually high or low price arising from genuine market activity is not an outlier.
A trader rushing to complete many trades before a long weekend is explicitly not considered a disorderly transaction.
relationships: These exceptions carve out which transactions are excluded when otherwise using primary/principal market prices for fair value.
trading_implications: Risk-limit-forced liquidations still count as valid market prices for mark-to-market purposes — a firm cannot argue its own forced unwind should be excluded as 'disorderly'.
common_misunderstandings: Internal-policy-driven forced liquidation (e.g., breaching risk limits) is not a 'forced sale' in the accounting sense, even though it is forced from the trader's perspective.
A price being unusually high or low due to normal market moves does not make it an outlier/erroneous price to be excluded.
related_topics: Market as a whole is never distressed

items.topic: The market as a whole is never considered distressed
items.definition: An accounting principle stating that even in a market-wide crash, published prices must still be used for fair value rather than substituted with a hold-to-maturity or normal-conditions valuation.
items.core_idea: Distress/forced-sale exceptions apply only to individual transactions, never to the market overall — as long as the market is open and participants could transact, published prices are mandatory for fair value, even during a crash.
key_points: It is not acceptable to value an asset via a hold-to-maturity approach (discounting expected future cash flows) as a workaround during a market decline.
It is also not acceptable to substitute assumptions based on 'normal' market conditions when the real market is stressed.

The FASB definition (ASC 820-10-35-51D) reaffirms that fair value remains the orderly-transaction exit price under CURRENT market conditions, even after a significant decrease in volume/activity, regardless of which valuation technique is used.
relationships: Complements the disorderly-transaction exceptions: those exclude specific bad trades, but never let a firm treat the whole market as invalid.
trading_implications: During a market crash, a trading desk cannot mark its book off a discounted-cash-flow / hold-to-maturity model to smooth out mark-to-market losses; it must still use actual current market prices.
common_misunderstandings: A crashing or highly volatile market is not, by itself, grounds to abandon published prices in favor of a theoretical or historical-conditions valuation.

items.definition: A three-tier classification (ASC 820 / IFRS 13) of the inputs used to value assets and liabilities, ranging from highly observable exchange prices to unobservable, illiquid-market estimates.
items.core_idea: Because fair value must be estimated even for illiquid positions lacking regular pricing, accounting standards require firms to disclose how liquid/observable their valuation inputs are, using a three-level input hierarchy; an asset's own level classification is set by the least-observable input it relies on.
key_points: Level 1 inputs are highly observable — typically prices taken directly from an exchange.
Level 2 inputs are more subjective, often arising from fragmented markets where trading activity is spread across multiple venues.
Level 3 inputs are unobservable, associated with markets that have limited liquidity.
A security is classified as level 1 if it's valued exclusively with level 1 inputs.
A security is level 2 if it uses a combination of level 1 and level 2 inputs.
A security is level 3 if it incorporates at least one level 3 input — i.e., the classification is driven by the least-liquid input used, not the majority of inputs.
relationships: Exists because exit price only requires an orderly market (not an active one), so many positions must be valued without regular market pricing — the hierarchy standardizes how that uncertainty is disclosed to shareholders.
trading_implications: A single unobservable (level 3) input pulls the entire security's classification down to level 3, even if every other input is level 1 — firms should be aware one illiquid component can drive the disclosed valuation uncertainty for an otherwise liquid instrument.
common_misunderstandings: Level classification is not an average or majority vote across inputs — using even one level 3 input makes the whole security level 3.
